'''Catherine S. Woolley''' (born July 30, 1965) is an American [[neuroendocrinologist]]. Woolley holds the William Deering Chair in Biological Sciences in the Department of Neurobiology, Weinberg College of Arts & Sciences, at [[Northwestern University]].<ref name="Northwestern">{{cite web |title=Catherine Woolley |url=https://www.neurobiology.northwestern.edu/people/core-faculty/catherine-woolley.html |website= Northwestern University |access-date=29 September 2018}}</ref><ref name="Fralin">{{cite web |title=Brain Estrogens and Epilepsy: Evidence for latent sex differences in mechanisms of neuromodulation |url=https://fralin.vt.edu/VTLSS/fall-2018/7.html |website=Fralin Life Science Institute |publisher=Virginia Tech |access-date=2 October 2018}}</ref>
She is also a member of the Women's Health Research Institute in the [[Feinberg School of Medicine]] at Northwestern University.<ref name="Biospace">{{cite news |title=Another Difference Between The Sexes Uncovered, Northwestern University Reveals |url=https://www.biospace.com/another-difference-between-the-sexes-uncovered-northwestern-university-reveals |access-date=1 October 2018 |work=Biospace |date=August 14, 2015}}</ref>

Woolley studies cellular and [[molecular neuroscience]] in relation to the brain and behavior, particularly neuroendocrinology and the plasticity of neural circuits.<ref name="Northwestern"/> 
She attempts to understand molecular mechanisms of estrogen and its interactions with the structure and function of synapses in the adult brain, and their behavioral consequences.<ref name="Transformative"/> 
She has been described as "a leading authority in a very exciting area of adult neuroplasticity".<ref name="Azmitia"/>
Her earliest work included a pioneering study demonstrating that [[estrogen]] caused structural changes to cells in the rat hippocampus.<ref name="Garcia-Segura"/>  She has also shown that neuronal mechanisms in the rat brain differ in males and females. Her work has broad significance for drug development and women's health,<ref name="Shah"/> and for the studies of [[epilepsy]],<ref name="Paul">{{cite web |last1=Paul |first1=Marla |title=Researcher Explores Estrogen's Effect on Seizures May 8, 2007 |url=https://www.northwestern.edu/newscenter/stories/2007/05/epilepsy.html |website=Northweastern News |access-date=3 October 2018}}</ref> [[anxiety]]<ref name="Northwestern"/><ref name="Shansky">{{cite journal |last1=Shansky |first1=Rebecca M. |last2=Woolley |first2=Catherine S. |title=Considering Sex as a Biological Variable Will Be Valuable for Neuroscience Research |journal=The Journal of Neuroscience |date=23 November 2016 |volume=36 |issue=47 |pages=11817–11822 |doi=10.1523/JNEUROSCI.1390-16.2016 |pmid=27881768 |pmc=5125240 }}</ref> and [[Depression (mood)|depression]].<ref name="Lambert">{{cite book |last1=Lambert |first1=Kelly |title=Lifting depression : a neuroscientist's hands-on approach to activating your brain's healing power |date=2010 |publisher=Basic Books |isbn=978-0465018147 |pages=124–125 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6EIHhbEUVMEC&pg=PA124 |access-date=3 October 2018}}</ref>

==Early life==
Catherine S. Woolley was born on July 30, 1965, in [[Nelsonville, Ohio]]. She graduated from [[Texas A&M University]] in [[College Station, Texas]], with a B.Sc. honors in [[zoology]]<ref name="Azmitia">{{cite journal |last1=Azmitia |first1=Efrain C. |title=Krieg Cortical Kudos 2000 |url=https://academic.oup.com/cercor/article-pdf/10/8/826/9751081/100826.pdf |journal=Cerebral Cortex |date= 2000|volume=10|issue=8 |pages=826–828| doi= 10.1093/cercor/10.8.826 |pmid=10920054 |doi-access=free }}</ref> and was given a prize by the university for the best undergraduate honors thesis.<ref name="Stein">{{cite news |last1=Stein |first1=Anne |title=Staying in STEM Encouraging Women to Persist in Math and Science |url=https://www.weinberg.northwestern.edu/after-graduation/weinberg-magazine/spring-summer-2014/staying-in-stem.html |access-date=3 October 2018 |work=Weinberg College of Arts & Sciences |date=2014}}</ref>

==Career==
Woolley studied with [[Bruce McEwen]] at [[Rockefeller University]], receiving her Ph.D. from Rockefeller in 1993.<ref name="Fralin"/><ref name="Bear">{{cite book |editor-last1=Bear |editor-first1=Mark F. |editor-last2=Connors |editor-first2=Barry W. |editor-last3=Paradiso |editor-first3=Michael A. |title=Neuroscience : exploring the brain |date=2007 |publisher=Lippincott Williams & Wilkins |location=Baltimore, MD |isbn=978-1451109542 |edition=Fourth |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=75NgwLzueikC&pg=PA558 |chapter=Sex and the brain |journal=978-1451109542 |pages=555–558 }}</ref>
She did postdoctoral work at the [[University of Washington]] with Philip Schwartzkroin in the Department of Neurological Surgery.<ref name="Fralin"/>

In 1998, she became an assistant professor at [[Northwestern University]] in [[Illinois (State)|Evanston]].<ref name="Fralin"/> In 2013, Woolley was appointed to the William Deering Chair in Biological Sciences in the Department of Neurobiology, Weinberg College of Arts & Sciences, Northwestern University.<ref name="Northwestern"/>  She is the founding Director of Northwestern University's undergraduate Neuroscience program, and was named a Charles Deering McCormick Professor of Teaching Excellence by Northwestern in 2018 for "transforming the landscape of undergraduate education in Weinberg."<ref name="Deering2018">{{cite web |title=2018 Recipients |url=https://www.northwestern.edu/provost/faculty-honors/university-teaching-awards/award-recipients/2018.html#woolley |website=Northwestern University |access-date=2 October 2018}}</ref>

She was elected to the Council of the [[Society for Neuroscience]] (2014–2018).<ref>{{cite web |title=Volunteer Leadership |url=http://auth.brainfacts.sfn.org/SfN/About/Volunteer-Leadership |website=Society for Neuroscience |access-date=2 October 2018}}</ref> She is a senior editor of ''[[The Journal of Neuroscience]]''.<ref>{{cite web |title=2018 Editorial Board |url=http://www.jneurosci.org/content/editorial-board2 |website=The Journal of Neuroscience |access-date=2 October 2018}}</ref>

==Research==
===Rockefeller University===
[[Bruce McEwen]] at [[Rockefeller University]] studies stress and its impact on the  brain.<ref name="McEwen2017"/>
With McEwen, Woolley initially studied [[neuroleptics]] and their effects on [[proenkephalin]] [[mRNA]] levels.<ref name="Azmitia"/>
Woolley went on to work with McEwen and [[Elizabeth Gould (psychologist)|Elizabeth Gould]] on a 1990 study that examined the brain using [[Golgi's method]],<ref name="Azmitia"/><ref name="Garcia-Segura"/><ref name="Woolley1990a"/> a technique first described by [[Camillo Golgi]] in 1873.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Origins of neuroscience : a history of explorations into brain function|last=Finger|first=Stanley|publisher=Oxford University Press|year=1994|isbn=9780195146943|pages=45|oclc=27151391|quote=In 1873, Golgi published the first brief but "adequate" picture of ''la reazione nera'' (the black reaction), which showed the whole nerve cell, including its cell body, axon, and branching dendrites.}}</ref>
The study showed that [[estradiol]] increased the number and density of excitatory synapses of CA1 pyramidal cells in the rat hippocampus, as well as the density of dendritic spines. Both estradiol and spine density fluctuated dramatically during the [[estrous cycle]].<ref name="Azmitia"/><ref name="Garcia-Segura"/><ref name="Woolley1990a">{{cite journal |last1=Woolley |first1=CS |last2=Gould |first2=E |last3=Frankfurt |first3=M |last4=McEwen |first4=BS |title=Naturally occurring fluctuation in dendritic spine density on adult hippocampal pyramidal neurons. |journal=The Journal of Neuroscience |date=December 1990 |volume=10 |issue=12 |pages=4035–9 |pmid=2269895 |pmc=6570039 |doi=10.1523/JNEUROSCI.10-12-04035.1990 }}</ref> Woolley recognized that this suggested that the adult brain was subject to change, at least in rats; this was surprising because it was accepted at that time that the adult brain was structurally stable.<ref name="Azmitia"/><ref name="Bear"/><ref name="McEwen2017">{{cite journal |last1=McEwen |first1=Robert |title=When is stress good for you? |journal=AEON |date=11 July 2017 |url=https://aeon.co/essays/how-stress-works-in-the-human-body-to-make-or-break-us |access-date=2 October 2018}}</ref> Woolley's 1990 work is considered a pioneering study in hormones and [[brain plasticity|synaptic plasticity]].<ref name="Garcia-Segura">{{cite book |last1=Garcia-Segura |first1=Luis Miguel |title=Hormones and brain plasticity |date=May 5, 2009 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=9780195326611 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xzTiBwAAQBAJ&pg=PT107 |access-date=1 October 2018}}</ref>
Further work established that the manipulation of female 
sex hormones affects hippocampal structure in adult rats.<ref name="Garcia-Segura"/><ref name="Gould1990">{{cite journal |last1=Gould |first1=Elizabeth |last2=Woolley |first2=Catherine S. |last3=Frankfurt |first3=Maya |last4=McEwen |first4=Bruce S. |title=Gonadal Steroids Regulate Dendritic Spine Density in Hippocampal Pyramidal Cells in Adulthood |journal=The Journal of Neuroscience |date=1990 |volume=10 |issue=4 |pages=1286–1291 |url=https://www.princeton.edu/~goulde/pubs/Gonadal%20steroids%20regulate%20dendritic%20spine%20density%20in%20hippocampal%20pyramidal%20cells%20in%20adulthood.pdf |access-date=2 October 2018|doi=10.1523/JNEUROSCI.10-04-01286.1990 |pmid=2329377 |pmc=6570209 }}</ref>

===University of Washington ===
Between 1993 and 1998, Woolley worked as a postdoc at the [[University of Washington]] in Seattle, with Philip Schwartzkroin. There she applied electrophysiology techniques and ultrastructural analysis to the study of hormonal effects in the brain.<ref name="Azmitia"/><ref name="Woolley1999">{{cite journal |last1=Woolley |first1=CS |title=Electrophysiological and cellular effects of estrogen on neuronal function. |journal=Critical Reviews in Neurobiology |date=1999 |volume=13 |issue=1 |pages=1–20 |pmid=10223521 |doi=10.1615/CritRevNeurobiol.v13.i1.10 }}</ref><ref name="Stafstrom">{{cite journal |last1=Stafstrom |first1=Carl E. |title=Issues in Clinical Epileptology: A View from the Bench. A Festschrift in Honor of Philip A. Schwartzkroin, PhD |journal=Epilepsy Currents |date=December 2013 |volume=13 |issue=6 |pages=291–296 |doi=10.5698/1535-7597-13.6.291 |pmid=24348132 |pmc=3854749 }}</ref>  She studied the effects of [[estrogen]] on the release of [[GABA]] in the [[hippocampus]].<ref name="Etgen">{{cite book |last1=Etgen |first1=Anne M. |last2=Pfaff |first2=Donald W. |title=Molecular mechanisms of hormone actions on behavior |date=2009 |publisher=Elsevier/Academic Press |isbn=978-0123749390 |page=43}}</ref> 
In 2000, she received the Cortical Explorer Award in recognition of her work on neuroanatomy and brain activity.<ref name="Azmitia"/>

{{blockquote|"Catherine is finding the same  neuronotrophic activation  by  steroids  whether  she  uses Golgi  staining  to  count  spines  or  the  electron  microscope  to visualize  synapses.  The  methods  are  more  sophisticated  and powerful, but the basic observation is the same." Cortical Explorer Award, 2000<ref name="Azmitia"/>}}

===Northwestern University===
At Northwestern University, Woolley's research concentrates on how steroids effect and regulate synaptic structure and their functions. Woolley uses a spectrum of different methods in their studies such as in vitro and vivo electrophysiology, and behavioral assays to observe how the subjects reacts.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Catherine Woolley: Department of Neurobiology - Northwestern University |url=https://neurobiology.northwestern.edu/people/core-faculty/woolley-catherine.html |access-date=2026-03-01 |website=neurobiology.northwestern.edu |language=en}}</ref> As a professor at Northwestern University, 
Woolley has done ongoing research into the sex-specific effects of [[estrogens]], [[GABAA receptors]], [[metabotropic glutamate receptors]], and endogenous [[cannabinoids]] and their roles as neuromodulators of brain development and function.<ref name="Galanopoulou">{{cite journal |last1=Galanopoulou |first1=Aristea S. |title=Stirring the Pot With Estrogens |journal=Epilepsy Currents |date=May 2013 |volume=13 |issue=3 |pages=129–131 |doi=10.5698/1535-7511-13.3.129 |pmid=23840172 |pmc=3697880 }}</ref><ref name="Spencer">{{cite journal |last1=Spencer |first1=Joanna L. |last2=Waters |first2=Elizabeth M. |last3=Romeo |first3=Russell D. |last4=Wood |first4=Gwendolyn E. |last5=Milner |first5=Teresa A. |last6=McEwen |first6=Bruce S. |title=Uncovering the mechanisms of estrogen effects on hippocampal function |journal=Frontiers in Neuroendocrinology |date=May 2008 |volume=29 |issue=2 |pages=219–237 |doi=10.1016/j.yfrne.2007.08.006 |pmid=18078984 |pmc=2440702 }}</ref><ref name="Wissman">{{cite journal |last1=Wissman |first1=Anne Marie |last2=May |first2=Renee M. |last3=Woolley |first3=Catherine S. |title=Ultrastructural analysis of sex differences in nucleus accumbens synaptic connectivity |journal=Brain Structure and Function |date=11 October 2011 |volume=217 |issue=2 |pages=181–190 |doi=10.1007/s00429-011-0353-6 |pmid=21987050 |pmc=3275686 }}</ref>
In 2012, Woolley published research showing that estrogens had differential effects in the brains of female and male rats, decreasing inhibitory synaptic transmission in female rats but not in males.<ref name="Biospace"/><ref name="Huang">{{cite journal |last1=Huang |first1=Guang Zhe |last2=Woolley |first2=Catherine S. |title=Estradiol Acutely Suppresses Inhibition in the Hippocampus through a Sex-Specific Endocannabinoid and mGluR-Dependent Mechanism |journal=Neuron |date=June 2012 |volume=74 |issue=5 |pages=801–808 |doi=10.1016/j.neuron.2012.03.035|pmid=22681685 |pmc=3372866 }}</ref>
In 2015, her group reported that male and female rats differ in the molecular pathways affected by [[endocannabinoids]]. In female rats the drug [[URB-597]] increased the inhibitory effect of the endocannabinoid  [[anandamide]], lessening the release of neurotransmitters. In male rats, the drug had no effect. The interaction did not reflect circulating reproductive hormones.<ref name="Biospace"/> Further research is needed to determine the extent to which rat neurology provides an accurate model for human neurology.<ref name="Biospace"/><ref name="Shansky"/>

While the significance of these results for humans are not yet demonstrated, rats are often used as a model for studying humans.  An important implication of Woolley's research is that drug testing on males should not be assumed to yield   results applicable to both males and females. To understand drug action, effects on both sexes should be studied.<ref name="Biospace"/><ref name="Shah">{{cite web |last1=Shah |first1=Aparna |title=Sex differences in preclinical neuroscience research: Snippets from #SfN15 with Catherine Woolley |url=https://blogs.plos.org/neuro/2015/10/29/sex-differences-in-preclinical-neuroscience-research-snippets-from-sfn15-with-catherine-woolley-by-aparna-shah/ |website=PLOS Neuro Community |access-date=3 October 2018|date= October 29, 2015}}</ref><ref name="Shansky"/>
